name: Endermologie / LPG

lead: Endermologie, made by the French company LPG, is a motorised roller-and-suction massage treatment used to soften the look of cellulite and improve body contour.

The device pulls and rolls the skin with suction and rollers, a mechanical massage of the tissue beneath. Small studies of tens to a hundred or so women, including 33 and 118 participants, assessed cellulite grade and body measurements after about 15 sessions over several weeks. It is also used for lymphedema alongside compression.

paras: It is a course of roughly 15 sessions, around twice weekly, in a clinic or spa.
The sources describe it as FDA-approved as a massage system and do not detail adverse events. Larger controlled studies were not found among them.

angle.text: It is used to soften the look of cellulite and improve body contour: machine massage works the skin and tissue beneath, leaving smoother texture. Small studies report contour and texture changes, and large controlled evidence is limited.

lead: Endermologie, produced by the French company LPG, is a machine-assisted massage system that rolls the skin between motorised rollers while applying suction, intended to improve the look of cellulite and body contour [1]. Clients typically book a course of sessions in which a therapist glides the handpiece over the thighs, buttocks, hips or abdomen, in a suit that protects the skin, to smooth the surface and tighten the look of the area.

It was originally developed in the late 1970s in France to soften scars and standardise physical therapy, and clinicians then noticed changes in contour and skin texture in treated patients [1]. The technique is described as a motorised, rhythmic folding and unfolding of the fatty layer under the skin combined with suction [2].

Small clinical studies have evaluated it. One study of 33 women with cellulite gave 15 sessions twice weekly, and another of 118 women used a similar schedule; both assessed cellulite grade and body measurements [3][4]. A 1999 randomised controlled trial compared it with aminophylline cream, and a 2011 study took fat biopsies to examine what the massage does inside the tissue [5][6]. It has also been explored for lymphedema in combination with compression bandaging, a medical rather than cosmetic use [7][8].

Described as FDA-approved as a massage system

paras: The system applies positive-pressure rolling together with negative pressure to skin and subcutaneous tissue [1]. A 1998 report states it was developed in France in the late 1970s for scars and physical therapy, and that its body-contour use followed from observed effects of treatment [1]. Since then machines have been used in France, the United States and elsewhere for cellulite and contour, and that report describes the device as FDA-approved as a massage system [1].

Cellulite, per Wikipedia, is herniation of subcutaneous fat within fibrous connective tissue that gives skin a dimpled look on the buttocks, thighs and abdomen; it is estimated to affect 80 to 90 percent of post-adolescent women of European descent and is described as believed to be physiological rather than pathological [9][9]. The article lists mechanical suction and massage among non-invasive options and says cellulite can resist many treatments [9][9].

The handpiece lifts a fold of skin between two rollers while suction draws tissue into the head, producing a rhythmic folding and unfolding of the fat layer [2]. A 2011 study of 12 premenopausal women used biopsies and microdialysis of thigh fat before and after 12 sessions of mechanical massage over about six weeks; it reported changes in gene expression, enhanced lipid mobilisation after a lipolytic agent, and improved local blood flow [6]. A 1999 report found that a single 40-minute session produced no noticeable change in most blood parameters, but plasma estradiol varied significantly, falling during the session and rising afterwards; the authors compared this with clinical observations of a trophic effect on skin and connective tissue [2].

Studies differ in design and in what they measured. The 1998 one-year outcome update reported on body contouring [1]. A 2009 study treated 33 healthy women with grade 1 to 3 cellulite twice weekly for 15 sessions, assessing photographs and circumference measurements [3], and a 2013 study enrolled 118 women on the same schedule and evaluated cellulite grade, safety and slimming [4].

A 1999 randomised controlled trial in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery compared twice-weekly endermologie with aminophylline cream over 12 weeks in 52 women who completed it; the abstract reports no statistical difference in measurements between treated and control legs in any group, and that patients' own assessments were mostly unchanged [5]. A 2001 report compared endermologie after ultrasound-assisted liposuction with liposuction alone [10]. A 1997 article asked whether the treatment works [11].

sections.h: Cellulite and where mechanical massage fits
paras: Endermologie is mostly used on cellulite, the dimpled look of skin over the thighs, buttocks and abdomen. Wikipedia cites one review giving prevalence of 85 to 98 percent among women of European descent, and says it is considerably less common in women of East Asian descent and rarely seen in men.[9] The article lists proposed contributors including genetics, sex, body type, fat distribution and circulatory function, and says an oestrogen-progesterone imbalance has been proposed without reliable clinical support.[9]

The same article places mechanical suction and mechanical massage among non-invasive options, alongside topical creams, collagenase injections, and energy-based devices using radiofrequency, ultrasound, cryotherapy, laser or pulsed light, and notes that combinations of mechanical and energy-based treatments are widely used and that cellulite can be resistant to many treatments.[9] It gives no effectiveness figures for mechanical massage itself, so the trials below are the main published measurements.
The abstracts available describe the device as FDA-approved as a massage system and do not detail adverse events [1][3][4]. The 2013 study evaluated safety alongside slimming outcomes [4].

In lymphedema, a 2007 report presented two protocols combining the system with compression bandaging in women with secondary arm lymphedema [7]. A phase II randomised trial protocol was published in 2019 for breast-cancer-related lymphedema [8], and a registered trial (n=93, started 2015) concerns a treatment pathway for breast cancer related lymphoedema [12].

A 1998 outcome study reported one-year results of treatment for body contouring [1]. A 2009 study treated 33 healthy women with grade 1 to 3 cellulite twice weekly for 15 sessions, assessing photographs and circumference measurements [3]. A 2013 study enrolled 118 women on the same schedule and evaluated cellulite grade, safety and slimming [4]. A 1999 randomised trial of 52 completers compared it with aminophylline cream [5]. A 2011 clinical study of 12 women examined gene expression and lipid mobilisation in thigh fat [6].

In lymphedema, a 2007 report presented two protocols combining the system with compression bandaging in women with secondary arm lymphedema, a phase II randomised trial protocol was published in 2019 for breast cancer related lymphedema, and a registered trial of a treatment pathway for breast cancer related lymphoedema exists [7][8][12].
